name: Papaya enzyme hair inhibitor

lead: Folk and cosmetic-marketing advice holds that applying papaya or its papain enzyme after hair removal weakens hair and slows regrowth, leaving less visible body hair.

Papain is a protein-digesting enzyme from papaya, used in meat tenderisers, wound debridement and some cosmetics. Proponents reason it could degrade hair protein or follicle structures. No published study located tested the hair claim.

paras: People apply papaya pulp or papain-containing products to the skin after waxing or shaving, repeating it as part of their hair-removal routine.

In 2008 the US FDA moved against marketing of unapproved topical papain drug products, citing reports of allergic reactions causing low blood pressure and rapid heart rate. People with latex allergy may be at higher risk of reacting to topical papain.

angle.text: Folk advice says papaya's papain enzyme, applied after hair removal, slows regrowth so body hair is less visible. The enzyme is well characterised; no published trials test the hair claim.

lead: The papaya enzyme hair inhibitor is the idea that applying papaya, or its enzyme papain, to the skin after hair removal slows regrowth, so smooth skin lasts longer between waxing or epilation sessions. It appears in post-wax products marketed as hair-regrowth retardants, and the claim also circulates as a home remedy.[1]

Papain, also called papaya proteinase I, is a cysteine protease from papaya (Carica papaya). It has established uses in meat tenderizers, wound debridement, cosmetics and other industries.[2] Product marketing describes papain as having long been used to prolong hair removal results; one retailer's blog post on a post-epilation papaya concentrate cites no study for this.[1] Proponents' reasoning is that a protein-digesting enzyme might weaken hair or follicle structures.
No published human trial of papain or papaya for slowing hair regrowth was found, and Wikipedia's papain article does not discuss hair products.[2]

paras: Papain is the namesake of the papain-like protease family. Beyond food and cosmetics, it is used to dissociate tissue in cell-culture work and in Papacarie, a gel for removing tooth decay without drilling.[2] Wikipedia lists cosmetics as one of several industries using the enzyme, without describing hair-related uses.[2]

A retailer's post on a papaya-and-vitamin-E post-epilation ampoule says the product helps slow hair regrowth and describes papain as long used to prolong the effects of hair removal; the post gives no study or results.[1]

On September 23, 2008, the US FDA warned companies to stop marketing topical papain drug products sold without approval, citing reports of serious drops in blood pressure with increased heart rate. People allergic to latex can also be allergic to papaya, so those with latex sensitivity may face a higher risk of reaction to topical papain.[2]
No studies found testing papain or papaya for slowing hair regrowth.
